prompt: is it wrong to lie to a dying person? essay pls

So my grandmother has dementia and every time she asks where my grandfather is, we tell her he's at the hardware store. He died in 2019. My aunt thinks this is cruel and that we should tell her the truth each time, even if it means she grieves fresh every afternoon. I think the kind lie is obviously right but I can't fully say why, and the 'obviously' is bothering me. Could you write an essay that takes my aunt's side seriously before landing wherever it lands? Around 1200 words. Doesn't have to agree with me.

Write a short essay arguing that envy is an underrated moral emotion: that it tells you something true about what you value, and that people who claim never to feel it are either lying or have stopped wanting things.
Why do we feel worse about breaking a promise to a stranger than a promise to ourselves? I break promises to myself constantly and nobody cares, including me. Write it up as an essay.

I would like an essay of roughly 1,500 words on the ethics of anonymous kidney donation to strangers. Specifically: if it is admirable but not obligatory, what does that tell us about the concept of supererogation, and is that concept doing honest work or just letting the rest of us off the hook?

blog post idea: 'the case for being a little bit boring.' I'm 34, I quit trying to have interesting opinions about everything, and I'm happier. Want something that argues this isn't just giving up. Conversational, maybe 800 words.

I keep thinking about this and maybe it's dumb. If I eat meat but would never kill an animal myself, am I a hypocrite, or is the division of labor morally fine the way it's fine that I don't build my own house? I'd really appreciate an essay that thinks this through honestly, without just scolding me or letting me off. Sorry if that's a weird ask.

Essay prompt for myself that I'd like you to draft: Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' objection is usually aimed at impartialist ethics. I want to argue it cuts just as hard against virtue ethics, because the virtuous agent who saves his wife 'because that's what a loving husband does' has also had one thought too many. 1000-1500 words, assume a reader who has taken one ethics course.
Op-ed: tipping is a moral mess. Argue it.

I'm a hospice nurse. People assume the hardest thing about my job is death, but it's actually watching families negotiate what the patient 'would have wanted' when they clearly mean what they want. Write a personal essay in my voice about the ethics of speaking for someone who can't speak anymore. First person, honest, not sentimental. ~1000 words.
Write something exploring why we find it creepier to be watched by a person than by a camera, even when the camera records everything and the person forgets in five minutes.
Why politeness is underrated as a moral virtue. Not kindness, not compassion — plain, slightly fake politeness. I want an essay that defends it against the charge of being shallow.

ok so there's this thought experiment I can't shake. if you could take a pill that made you perfectly content with your current life, same job, same apartment, same everything, but you'd lose any desire to improve it, would you take it? my roommate says yes instantly. I say no but my reasons sound kind of snobbish when I say them out loud. essay? like 1000 words, take it wherever

Please write an essay considering whether we owe anything to people who will exist in 500 years, given that our choices determine which specific people come to exist at all. I am familiar with Parfit's non-identity problem and would prefer the essay not simply summarize it but attempt to say something about what follows for ordinary decisions like having children.
Essay: is boredom a moral failing?

What I wish I knew about forgiveness before I tried to do it. Write this as a personal essay. Context: I spent about two years 'forgiving' my brother for something, announced it to him, and then realized I hadn't. Turns out forgiveness isn't a decision. Or is it? You tell me.

Write a persuasive essay arguing that we should judge people more by their habits than their choices. Big dramatic choices get all the attention in ethics, but who you are is mostly what you do on a Tuesday.

Can you be a good person and a bad friend? I mean genuinely ethical in public life, generous to causes, but flaky, distracted, forgetful with the people closest to you. I suspect I know a few people like this and I might be one. Essay length, whatever feels right.

I teach high school philosophy. I want a model essay (around 900 words) my students could read on whether luck undermines moral responsibility. The drunk driver who hits a child versus the equally drunk driver who gets home safely. Pitched at smart 17-year-olds, no jargon without explanation, and it should actually take a position.
Is it ever okay to read your teenager's texts? Write an essay. I'm a parent and I want the real argument, not a parenting article.

an essay on the ethics of quitting. we praise persistence so much, but sometimes walking away from a commitment (a PhD, a marriage, a band) is the more honest act. where's the line between integrity and stubbornness?
Make the case that gratitude journaling is a little bit morally suspect: that listing what you're thankful for every night can quietly turn other people into props in your self-improvement project.
Why do we admire people who die for causes we think are wrong?

My dad was a lawyer who defended some genuinely awful people and he always said everyone deserves a defense, which, fine. But he also seemed to enjoy winning those cases a little too much, and I've never figured out whether the enjoyment matters morally if the action was right. Like does your motive matter if the system needs someone to do the thing anyway? Could you write an essay about that, maybe 1200-1500 words? Don't make it about my dad specifically.
Op-ed, about 700 words: we should stop calling billionaires' donations 'generosity.' Argue it but be fair to the other side.
Essay on why semicolons make people so angry.

I learned English at 19 after moving from Lviv, and I still dream in Ukrainian but I argue in English. I'd love a personal essay, first person as if it's me, about how the language you fight in might not be the language you love in. Around 1000 words. Keep it grounded, specific, not a TED talk.
Write an essay arguing that 'show, don't tell' is the most overrated piece of writing advice, and that some of the best prose in English is almost pure telling.

why do some words become embarrassing to say out loud? 'moist' is the obvious one but also 'panties', 'journey' (when used about personal growth), 'synergy'. Write something exploring what's going on there.

I would appreciate an essay on whether a translation can ever be better than its original, and if so, what 'better' could even mean. Examples from poetry welcome, but I'm more interested in the conceptual question.

for my newsletter (mostly librarians and teachers, ~3k subscribers): an essay on rereading. why the second time through a book is often the first time you actually read it. warm but not twee, 800ish words

I've been writing a novel for six years and I'm starting to think finishing it would ruin it, because right now it can still be good in my head. Is that cowardice or is there something real there? Could you write an essay on the unfinished book as a kind of comfort? I don't need encouragement, I need someone to think about it with me.

Draft an essay making the argument that the em dash has quietly replaced the semicolon as the default mark of a 'literary' sentence, and that this shift reflects a change from logical to conversational prose. I'm a copyeditor of 15 years so don't be cute about punctuation; I want an actual argument with examples.
Is Moby-Dick boring on purpose? Essay.
What I wish I'd known about writing before my MFA, which cost me $68,000 and taught me mostly how to sit in a circle. Personal essay, funny but not bitter. Or a little bitter.
Write an essay about why villains get the best lines. Milton's Satan, Iago, Hannibal Lecter. Is it because evil is more articulate, or because writers secretly side with them?
Argue that the second person ('you') is the most manipulative point of view in fiction, and that this is exactly why it works.

My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.

An essay, please, on the ethics of publishing a dead writer's work against their wishes. Kafka asked Max Brod to burn everything. Brod refused, and we have The Trial. Was Brod right, and does our gratitude settle the question?
Write a personal essay about keeping a diary for twenty years and then rereading it, and finding that the person in it is a stranger who annoys you. What is a diary for, if not for the future self?
Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.

I run a translation agency. Write an essay on why jokes are the hardest thing to translate, harder than poetry, and what that suggests about what humor actually is. Use real-ish examples (puns, timing, cultural reference) but keep the focus on the idea. 1200 words.
what's the deal with people who say they 'don't read fiction because it's not real'? I want an essay that takes them seriously for a minute before explaining what they're missing

Op-ed for a regional paper: our town's library is replacing its reference desk with self-checkout kiosks. Write an essay about what is lost when you stop being able to ask a stranger a question about a book. 600-750 words, no nostalgia porn.

Write something exploring why we read the same bedtime story to children a hundred times and they never get tired of it, while adults find repetition unbearable. What are kids getting that we've lost?
An essay arguing that the best writing advice ever given is 'read it out loud' and that almost every other rule is a special case of it.

I'm a court stenographer. For 22 years I've typed other people's words exactly, including their ums and broken sentences, and I've come to think spoken language is far stranger and more beautiful than written. Write a personal essay from my perspective about what transcription teaches you about how people actually talk.

Write an essay about the words that exist in one language and not in another, but skip the usual listicle stuff (hygge, saudade, etc). I want to know whether lacking a word actually stops you from feeling the thing, or just from talking about it.
Blog essay: why I stopped finishing books I don't like, and why it took me until 41 to give myself permission. Light tone, but I want a real point about what we owe authors (if anything).

Please write an essay of approximately 1,000 words on whether an author's private morality should affect how we read their work. I want to avoid the usual 'separate the art from the artist' framing and instead ask whether some works are actually changed, as texts, by what we learn about the person who wrote them.
